Newborn Care

When pumping hurts your nipples: finding the cause and relief

Updated: October 6, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Pumping may take practice, but it should not require you to endure nipple pain. Soreness can come from the pump, from an existing feeding injury or from a breast or skin condition that needs different treatment. Turning up the suction or buying another cream without checking the cause can prolong the problem. A comfortable fit and an observed pumping session are often useful starting points.

What pumping should feel like

A pump should create a comfortable, rhythmic pulling sensation. Some people notice tingling when milk begins to flow, and a very full breast may feel pressured before expression starts. Sharp pain, pinching, burning that persists, bleeding or worsening soreness should not be treated as the normal price of collecting milk.

Many pumps begin with a faster stimulation pattern and then switch to an expression pattern. Names and controls differ between models. A slower or deeper cycle does not mean that you must accept stronger suction; the useful setting is one that removes milk comfortably.

The nipple may lengthen temporarily in the tunnel as the pump works. Look for repeated rubbing, increasing swelling or an uncomfortable change in colour rather than expecting it to remain completely still. Persistent blanching, a white-to-purple colour change or burning after pumping may need assessment for compression or blood-vessel spasm.

If pumping hurts, reduce the setting or stop to reassess. Turn off the pump and release the seal gently before removing the flange. Pulling it away while suction is still active can add to the injury.

Check the flange while the pump is running

The flange, sometimes called a breast shield, is the part that sits against the breast and guides the nipple into a tunnel. Fit relates particularly to the nipple and how it moves during pumping, not simply to breast size or the diameter of the whole areola. The size supplied with the pump will not suit everyone.

A tunnel that is too narrow may squeeze or rub the nipple. A tunnel that is too wide may pull in an uncomfortable amount of areola and cause swelling. Either problem can make pumping painful, and pain can make it harder to settle into a productive session.

Centre the nipple before starting and check what happens under gentle suction. A static measurement can help choose a starting size, but comfort and movement during an actual session matter. The two breasts may need different sizes, and the fit may change over time.

A lactation professional can watch a session and help distinguish a sizing problem from high suction, poor positioning, swelling or another cause. There is no universal rule that every nipple needs the same extra number of millimetres. A larger flange is not automatically the answer to pain.

Review suction, assembly and the pump itself

Start with a low setting and increase only within a comfortable range if needed. Maximum suction is not a target, and pain is not evidence that the pump is doing a better job. A setting that was comfortable last week may need adjustment if the nipple is now injured or the breast is swollen.

Check the manufacturer’s instructions for assembly, seals, valves and other replaceable parts. A damaged or incorrectly fitted component may affect performance. If less milk is being collected, look at the whole situation before responding with stronger suction or a much longer session.

Position yourself so that you do not have to hold the flange at an awkward angle or press it hard into the breast. A hands-free bra should support the equipment without forcing the breast into an uncomfortable position. Comfort should be checked again after any change in equipment or posture.

If the pump appears to malfunction, contact the manufacturer and use an alternative feeding or expression plan agreed with your care team. Buying a different pump may sometimes help, but it should not replace an assessment of fit and technique.

Do not overlook pain that started during breastfeeding

A nipple already damaged by a shallow latch can also hurt during pumping. Switching from breast to pump does not immediately heal a crack or remove the cause of the original injury. If you do both, it is useful to have someone observe both feeding and pumping.

At the breast, comfortable attachment involves a deep mouthful of breast tissue, not a rule that every bit of the areola must fit inside the baby’s mouth. Areola size varies. Positioning, how the baby opens their mouth and how feeding feels all contribute to the assessment.

A midwife, breastfeeding specialist or appropriately qualified lactation consultant can help. If direct feeding is too painful, ask about gentle hand expression or another comfortable way to remove enough milk while the cause is treated. The aim is to protect feeding and milk production without repeatedly injuring the same area.

Fullness, engorgement and inflammation need a gentler approach

An engorged breast may feel tight and swollen, and the area around the nipple can become less easy for the baby or flange to work with. A small amount of gentle hand expression may soften the area or relieve discomfort. The goal is not to force the breast completely empty.

What is often called a blocked duct can involve narrowing and inflammation rather than a solid plug that needs to be pushed out. Deep massage, vibration and repeated extra pumping can worsen swelling and tissue injury. Prolonged heat is not a necessary treatment and may make inflammation worse.

Continue milk removal at a comfortable level that meets the baby’s needs or your established pumping plan. Avoid abruptly stopping and becoming very full, but also avoid adding repeated sessions solely to empty an inflamed breast. Ask for help adapting the plan if pain prevents adequate expression.

A wrapped cold pack or cool compress can soothe soreness. A clinician or pharmacist can advise on suitable pain relief, including when breastfeeding. An enlarging painful area, fever, flu-like symptoms or symptoms that fail to improve within about 12 to 24 hours need medical advice; seek help sooner if you feel very unwell.

Help damaged skin heal without adding more irritation

Once rubbing or excessive suction is corrected, protect the sore area from further friction. Clean it gently, avoid harsh soaps or scrubbing, and change damp breast pads. Check whether a new pad, detergent, nipple product or pump accessory coincided with the irritation.

There is no single cream proven to solve every kind of nipple pain. Research on treatments such as lanolin, dressings and all-purpose ointment has not established a clearly superior routine option, and studies of breastfeeding pain do not automatically answer every question about pumping injuries.

A small amount of expressed milk is sometimes suggested for a minor sore area, but it should not be presented as a treatment for infection or persistent damage. A crack that bleeds, does not heal or keeps returning needs the underlying cause assessed. The right treatment for dermatitis is different from treatment for a bacterial infection.

Repeated saline soaks and keeping damaged skin wet for long periods are not established necessities for healing. Avoid experimenting with several products at once, because this can make irritation and its cause harder to identify. A clinician may prescribe a targeted treatment when there is a specific diagnosis.

Be careful with oils, lubricants and nipple blebs

Some people try lubrication to reduce friction in the flange tunnel. Before applying a product, check that it is appropriate for breast contact, the baby and the pump materials. Ask a lactation professional or the manufacturer if unsure. Kitchen oils, fragranced products and essential oils should not be assumed suitable just because they are easy to obtain.

Lubrication should not disguise a poor fit or allow you to tolerate painful suction. If you need more and more product to get through a session, return to the fit and technique assessment. Do not apply a hot-oil or soaking regimen to treat an inflamed breast.

A small white spot on the nipple may be a bleb, but appearance alone does not identify every lesion. Do not pick, pierce or scrape it open. Persistent or painful spots need assessment so that inflammation, skin injury and other causes can be distinguished.

Burning or flaky nipples are not automatically thrush

Redness, shiny skin, flaking and burning have several possible causes. Friction, contact dermatitis, eczema, bacterial problems and blood-vessel spasm can overlap in appearance and symptoms. Persistent deep breast pain should not automatically be labelled a yeast infection.

If your baby has white patches in the mouth or feeding discomfort, have that assessed too. A baby’s oral symptoms and a parent’s nipple pain may be related, but one does not prove the diagnosis in the other. A clinician can decide whether either or both need treatment.

Antifungal treatment should follow an appropriate assessment rather than be the next step after every unsuccessful flange change. Probiotics are not an established treatment for nipple yeast infection. If a prescribed treatment is not helping, return for review instead of indefinitely repeating it.

Recognise signs that need medical assessment

A nipple crack does not automatically mean infection, but increasing pain, spreading redness or warmth, pus-like discharge, fever or feeling unwell should prompt medical advice. Mastitis can be inflammatory or bacterial, and treatment depends on the clinical picture.

A clinician may examine the nipple and breast, ask about feeding and pumping, and sometimes arrange additional tests. Antibiotics are useful when a bacterial infection is diagnosed or strongly suspected; they are not a routine treatment for every sore nipple. Do not start leftover tablets or someone else’s cream.

A persistent or enlarging painful lump can need assessment for an abscess or another problem. If treatment has been started but symptoms worsen or are not improving as expected, contact the prescriber. Severe illness, faintness, confusion or rapidly worsening symptoms requires urgent care.

In many situations breastfeeding or expression can continue, but the plan should reflect pain, milk removal and the treatment prescribed. Do not assume that every infection requires discarding milk or stopping suddenly. Ask your clinician for specific advice about any unusual discharge or the medicine you are using.

Keep the pump clean without trying to sterilise your skin

Wash your hands before handling the kit. After each use, take apart the components that contact milk and clean them according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Use suitable cleaning equipment and allow parts to air-dry fully in a clean place before storage.

CDC guidance recommends sanitising for extra protection, particularly when a baby is younger than two months, was born prematurely or has a weakened immune system. For an older, healthy baby, careful cleaning after each use may be sufficient without daily sanitising. Check any individual instructions from your baby’s medical team.

These steps protect collected milk from contamination. They do not mean that nipples need disinfectant or aggressive washing, which can irritate skin. Good equipment hygiene and comfortable pumping technique address different problems; one cannot compensate for neglecting the other.

What the research says about pump problems

A study published in 2014 analysed information from 1,844 mothers. About 62% reported a pump-related problem and 15% reported an injury; insufficient milk extraction and sore nipples were common reports. These figures describe that study population and equipment era, not the expected risk for every person using a pump today.

The study found associations with pump type and how people learned to pump. Because it was observational, it cannot prove that all battery-powered pumps cause injury or that a particular type is always the safest. Modern devices also vary substantially. Avoid choosing a pump solely from a simplified interpretation of one older survey.

Learning with another person was associated with fewer problems in the study. In practice, a skilled observer can spot something that written instructions cannot see, such as a nipple rubbing on one side or a flange pressed too firmly against the breast. Keep the manufacturer’s instructions, and add individual support when needed.

A practical plan for the next session

Before pumping again, check the skin, centre the nipple and begin with comfortable suction. Stop if pain returns rather than trying to complete a predetermined number of minutes. If needed, ask about a temporary expression and feeding plan that protects both the nipple and the baby’s intake.

Note when the pain occurs: at the start, throughout pumping, after removal or during direct feeding. Record any cracks, rash, colour change, fever or breast lump. Bring the pump, flanges and relevant products to a support appointment if possible, so the problem can be assessed in context.

Arrange help early for persistent pain, recurrent damage or difficulty collecting enough milk for your feeding plan. You do not have to wait until the nipple is bleeding or until work and sleep are being disrupted. A workable schedule, comfortable equipment and a clear review point are more useful than being told to keep pushing through.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Painful pumping calls for an assessment of fit, suction, technique and any underlying skin or breast condition. A sore nipple does not by itself establish thrush or bacterial infection.

For inflammation, current guidance favours gentle, appropriate milk removal over deep massage or repeated pumping to empty the breast. Persistent or systemic symptoms require medical review.

How BeMama can help

Make the next session comfortable and get someone to assess the actual pump fit when pain keeps returning.

When to seek help

Seek prompt medical advice for worsening breast pain, fever, spreading redness, pus-like discharge or a painful lump. Get urgent care if you feel severely unwell.

Evidence notes updated: October 6, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Pumping should not require enduring pain; check fit and settings early.
  • An existing latch injury or skin condition can also make pumping hurt.
  • Avoid deep massage, picking blebs and extra pumping solely to empty an inflamed breast.
  • Persistent injury or infection symptoms need professional assessment.

Frequently asked questions

Is nipple pain normal when I first use a pump?

A pulling sensation and learning period are expected, but sharp pain, persistent burning, bleeding or worsening soreness are reasons to adjust the setup and seek help. Do not treat pain as proof that the suction is effective.

How can I tell if the flange is too small or too large?

A narrow tunnel may squeeze or rub the nipple; a wide one may pull in too much areola and cause discomfort or swelling. Assess movement and comfort while pumping. The two breasts may need different sizes, and a professional can help check the fit.

Should I increase suction to collect more milk?

Only within a comfortable range, if needed. Maximum suction is not a goal. Pain or falling output should prompt a check of fit, parts, technique and the broader feeding situation rather than automatically using a stronger or longer cycle.

Can I pump while a nipple crack heals?

Sometimes, with a comfortable setup and an appropriate plan. Repeatedly rubbing the same injury can delay healing. Ask about fit changes, gentle hand expression or another temporary approach if pumping hurts, and get a persistent or bleeding crack assessed.

Should I massage a blocked duct hard or pump until empty?

No. Firm massage and extra pumping can aggravate inflammation. Use gentle milk removal appropriate to the baby’s needs or your established plan, and ask for advice if pain prevents it. Seek medical review for worsening symptoms or systemic illness.

Which cream will heal a sore nipple fastest?

There is no single best product for every cause. Friction, dermatitis and infection need different approaches. Correct the cause first and use any prescribed treatment as directed. Avoid combining multiple creams or assuming a general ointment will solve recurring damage.

Does burning mean I have thrush?

Not necessarily. Skin irritation, compression, blood-vessel spasm and other problems can cause burning. A clinician should assess persistent symptoms and any oral symptoms in your baby before deciding whether antifungal treatment is appropriate.

Can I open a white nipple spot with a needle?

No. Picking or piercing can cause injury and worsen inflammation. Have a persistent or painful spot assessed so that the cause and suitable treatment can be identified.

Do pump parts need sanitising after every session?

Clean milk-contact parts after every use. Sanitising is an additional step, particularly important for very young, premature or immunocompromised babies. Follow manufacturer and care-team guidance; sanitising equipment does not require disinfecting nipple skin.

When should I contact a clinician rather than keep adjusting the pump?

Get help for persistent pain, bleeding, a recurring crack or poor milk removal. Fever, increasing breast pain, spreading redness, pus-like discharge or a painful lump need prompt medical advice. Severe illness or rapidly worsening symptoms warrants urgent care.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
